'''John Francis Donoghue''' (born November 30, 1950) is an American theoretical physicist whose research primarily focuses on [[particle physics]],  [[general relativity]] and [[quantum gravity]], with a particular emphasis on the use of effective field theory methods. He is Distinguished Professor Emeritus at the [[University of Massachusetts Amherst]].

==Education and career==
John Donoghue was born on November 30, 1950, in [[Manhasset, New York]]. He received a B.S. in physics from the [[University of Notre Dame]] in 1972 and earned his Ph.D. in physics from the University of Massachusetts (UMass) Amherst in 1976, with [[Barry Holstein]] as his advisor. Following postdoctoral appointments at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] and [[Carnegie Mellon University]], Donoghue returned to UMass Amherst in 1980, where he spent the remainder of his academic career. He retired in 2015 but has continued his research.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://inspirehep.net/authors/1011544?ui-citation-summary=true|title=John F. Donoghue -- INSPIRE}}</ref>

==Research==
Donoghue began his career during a period marked by the discovery of the [[Charm quark|charm]] and [[bottom quarks]], initially focusing on the phenomenology of the [[quark model]]. His early work included studies of weak nonleptonic decays and tests of parity (P) and charge-parity (CP) symmetry violations.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Donoghue|first1=John F.|last2=Golowich|first2=Eugene|last3=Holstein|first3=Barry R.|date=1986|title=Low-energy weak interactions of quarks|journal=Physics Reports|volume=131|pages=319–428|doi=10.1016/0370-1573(86)90151-1|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0370157386901511?via%3Dihub|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He co-developed the Deplanques–Donoghue–Holstein (DDH) model<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Desplanques |first1=Bertrand|last2=Donoghue|first2=John F.|last3=Holstein|first3=Barry R.|date=February 1980|title=Unified treatment of the parity violating nuclear force|journal=Annals of Physics|volume=124|issue=2|pages=449–495|doi=10.1016/0003-4916(80)90217-1|bibcode=1980AnPhy.124..449D |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0003491680902171 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> (named after Bertrand Deplanques, Donoghue, and Barry Holstein)  for investigating parity non-conserving processes in nuclear interactions.

Donoghue’s work in particle phenomenology<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Donoghue|first1=John F.|last2=Ramirez|first2=Carlos|last3=Valencia|first3=GermanR.|date=April 1989|title=Spectrum of QCD and chiral Lagrangians of the strong and weak interactions|journal=Physical  Review D|volume=39|issue=7|pages=1947-1955|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.39.1947|url=https://journals.aps.org/prd/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevD.39.1947}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Burdman|first1=Gustavo|last2=Donoghue|first2=John F.|date=April 1992|title=Union of chiral and heavy quark symmetries|journal=Physics Letters B|volume=280|issue=3-4|pages=287-291|doi=10.1016/0370-2693(92)90068-F|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/037026939290068F}}</ref> also contributed to the development of [[chiral perturbation theory]], an effective field theory approach to low-energy [[quantum chromodynamics]].  These efforts were often conducted in collaboration with his UMass Amherst colleagues Barry Holstein and Eugene Golowich.

In the 1990s, building on his expertise in nonrenormalizable effective theories, Donoghue demonstrated that [[general relativity]] could be treated as an [[effective field theory]] at low energies.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Donoghue|first1=John F.|title=General relativity as an effective field theory: The leading quantum corrections|journal=Physical Review D |date=1994 |volume=50 |issue=6 |pages=3874–3888 |url=https://inspirehep.net/literature/38129|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.50.3874 |pmid=10018030 |arxiv=gr-qc/9405057 |bibcode=1994PhRvD..50.3874D }}</ref>  This work provided a framework for calculating quantum corrections to classical gravity in a model-independent way, without requiring a complete theory of quantum gravity.

In 1998, Donoghue co-authored a paper with V. Agrawal, S.M. Barr, and D. Seckel<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Agrawal|first1=V.|last2=Barr|first2=Stephen M.|last3=Donoghue|first3=John F.|last4=Seckel|first4=D.|title=Viable range of the mass scale of the standard model |journal=Physical Review D |date=1998 |volume=57 |issue=9 |pages=5480–5492 |url=https://inspirehep.net/literature/446049|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.57.5480 |arxiv=hep-ph/9707380 |bibcode=1998PhRvD..57.5480A }}</ref> that applied [[anthropic principle]] reasoning to the parameters of the [[Standard Model]], contributing to the concept of [[multiverse]] and the landscape of possible physical laws.

==Honors==
In 1989, Donoghue was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] for his “continued contributions to the theory and phenomenology of hadrons, especially in the studies of weak decays, CP violation, hadron spectroscopy, and chiral symmetry.”<ref>{{cite web |title=Division of Particles and Fields Fellowship |url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/aps-fellowship/dpf-fellowship |website=American Physical Society |access-date=16 August 2025}}</ref> In 2005, he was awarded the UMass Amherst Chancellor’s Medal,<ref>{{Cite web|title=UMass Amherst, College of Natural Sciences: Faculty Research Awards|url=https://www.umass.edu/physics/research/awards}}</ref>  and in 2011 was named a Distinguished Professor.<ref>{{Cite web|title=John Donoghue's official webpage at UMass Amherst|url=https://www.umass.edu/physics/about/directory/john-donoghue}}</ref> He was the recipient of the 2026 [[Sakurai Prize]] "for original and lasting contributions to the development of effective field theories, including work on gravity as an effective quantum field theory, and important contributions to chiral perturbation theory."<ref>{{Cite web|title=American Physical Society: J. J. Sakurai Prize for Theoretical Particle Physics|url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/prize/sakurai-prize}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=UMass Physicist John F. Donoghue Wins J.J. Sakurai Prize for Theoretical Particle Physics : UMass Amherst |url=https://www.umass.edu/news/article/umass-physicist-john-f-donoghue-wins-jj-sakurai-prize-theoretical-particle-physics |access-date=2026-11-07 |website=www.umass.edu |language=en}}</ref>

==Bibliography==
Donoghue is the author of over 300 scientific publications.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://inspirehep.net/authors/1011544?ui-citation-summary=true|title=John F. Donoghue -- INSPIRE}}</ref>

He has also co-authored two textbooks:

* The Dynamics of the Standard Model<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Donoghue|first1=John F.|last2=Golowich|first2=Eugene|last3=Holstein|first3=Barry R.|title=The Dynamics of the Standard Model|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/dynamics-of-the-standard-model/FF8A95F0F22A67FABA729DBB39BA2816 |publisher=Cambridge University Press|date=2023|doi=10.1017/9781009291033 |isbn=978-1-009-29103-3 }}</ref> (with Eugene Golowich and Barry Holstein)
* A Prelude to Quantum Field Theory<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Donoghue|first1=John |last2=Sorbo|first2=Lorenzo|title=A Prelude to Quantum Field Theory|url=https://press.princeton.edu/books/ebook/9780691223506/a-prelude-to-quantum-field-theory?srsltid=AfmBOooJ6O1KaPLHOHzhiPoO8J4s0wUXeLH8eNbkpou4AecuVf_0sLFe|date=2022|publisher=Princeton University Press |bibcode=2022pqft.book.....D }}</ref> (with Lorenzo Sorbo)
